failures.title: BMW N74B60 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Turbocharger Coolant Lines - Heat‑Related Leaks
items.whatHappens: The N74's hot‑vee layout places the turbos inside the V of the engine, generating extreme heat. The plastic coolant lines around the turbos become brittle and crack, leading to coolant loss. This is a well‑known issue on both the 6.0L and 6.6L N74 variants. If coolant loss is ignored, the engine can overheat and cause head gasket failure.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early, replacing the coolant lines is a labour‑intensive but manageable repair (£1,000-£2,000). If the engine has overheated, head gasket failure is likely - in which case a full replacement is often more cost‑effective. Read our full cooling system failure guide

items.title: Ignition Coil Failure - Misfires on V12
items.whatHappens: The N74's ignition coils are mounted under the intake manifold and are exposed to engine heat. They can fail, causing misfires, rough running, and check‑engine lights. On a V12, coil failure on one cylinder is noticeable and can lead to limp mode.
items.repairVsReplace: Coil replacement is a straightforward job (£300-£600 for all 12 coils) and does not require engine removal. However, accessing the coils requires removing the intake manifold, which adds labour. Read our full ignition coil failure guide

items.title: Injector & Fuel System Issues - High‑Pressure Pump Wear
items.whatHappens: The N74 uses a high‑pressure direct injection system. Injectors can become clogged or leak, and the high‑pressure fuel pump can wear over time. Symptoms include rough idle, hesitation, and fuel smell.
items.repairVsReplace: Injector replacement is a specialist job (£1,000-£2,000). Fuel pump replacement is also costly (£1,500-£3,000). If these issues are coupled with other problems, many owners opt for a reconditioned unit.

variants.title: N74B60 Sub‑Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: The N74B60 was produced in two main variants across the 7‑Series generations: the N74B60A (F‑series) and the N74B60B (G‑series). The differences are significant when buying a replacement. - Fitted to: F01/F02 760i / 760Li (2010-2015) - Key technical difference: 544 hp, 553 lb‑ft, earlier DME (engine management) version, different turbocharger actuators, 12‑valve ignition system design - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Shares the family coolant line and coil failure patterns; early production (2010-2012) had more frequent turbo coolant line issues - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with the N74B60B - ECU, wiring, turbo control and fuel system differ. Requires full electronics transplant if swapping between generations - Fitted to: G11/G12 760i / 760Li (2016-2022) - Key technical difference: Revised ECU calibration, updated turbocharger actuator design, improved cooling system routing, 535-544 hp depending on emissions calibration - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Improved coolant line materials but still shares the family ignition coil failure pattern; less prone to turbo coolant leaks than earlier A variant - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with earlier N74B60A - ECU, wiring and cooling system architecture differ. Use the correct variant for your chassis

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement N74B60 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used N74B60 is a risky proposition unless it comes from a very low‑mileage car with full documented history. The V12's complexity means many used engines have hidden issues (coolant leaks, coil failures, turbo wear). Only consider a used unit with proof of recent cooling system work and coil replacement. Factor in £2,000-£4,000 for preventative work if the history is unclear. Link once: /services/used-engines

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper N74B60 recon is the only sensible choice for owners of high‑value 7‑Series V12s. A quality recon should include: full strip and inspection, new coolant lines and water pumps, refurbished turbochargers, new ignition coils and injectors, new gaskets and seals, and a full test. With a 12-24 month warranty, this gives you a fresh engine with all known weaknesses engineered out - well worth the £8,000-£12,000 supply cost for a flagship BMW. Link once: /services/reconditioned-engines

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified when the original engine has suffered catastrophic failure (overheating, oil starvation) and the car is a cherished example (especially low‑mileage G‑series models). An upgraded rebuild should include new pistons/rings, refreshed cylinder heads, new timing chains and guides, and a full cooling system overhaul. This is specialist territory and typically only makes sense for cars with strong residual value (£30,000+). Link once: /services/rebuilt-engines

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: All engines can be supplied and fitted through our network of vetted BMW V12 specialists nationwide, with 12‑month warranty on reconditioned and rebuilt units. Link once: /services/supply-and-fit
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The N74B60 sits in F01/G11 760i - cars worth £10,000-£50,000 depending on age and condition. With a reconditioned supply cost of £8,000-£12,000, replacement is viable on higher‑value examples. However, for a high‑mileage F01 760i worth under £10,000, a used unit (£4,000-£7,000) may be the only sensible option - and even then, evaluate whether the car's overall condition justifies the spend. Given the V12's specialist nature, many owners choose to break the car rather than replace the engine if the value is low.

items.question: What are the most common failures on the N74B60?
items.answer: The most documented issues are turbocharger coolant line leaks (plastic lines cracking under heat), ignition coil failure (misfires on the V12), and high-pressure fuel pump/injector issues. The hot-vee design creates extreme heat that degrades plastic components and ignition coils over time. Coolant lines: replacement is strongly advised at 60k-100k miles. Ignition coils: failure is common; all 12 coils should be checked periodically. Fuel system: injectors and pump can wear, causing rough idle and hesitation.
bullets: Coolant lines: replacement is strongly advised at 60k‑100k miles.
Ignition coils: failure is common; all 12 coils should be checked periodically.
Fuel system: injectors and pump can wear, causing rough idle and hesitation.

items.question: Which BMW models use the N74B60 engine?
items.answer: The N74B60 was fitted exclusively to 7-Series models: F01/F02 760i/760Li (2010-2015, 544 hp) and G11/G12 760i/760Li (2016-2022, 535-544 hp). Not to be confused with the N73 (naturally aspirated predecessor) or the N74B66 (Rolls-Royce 6.6L). The N74B60 is BMW's last production V12 - the S68 V8 hybrid has replaced it.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned N74B60 engine?
items.answer: A used N74B60 is risky unless it comes from a very low-mileage car with full documented history and proof of recent cooling system work. The V12's complexity means many used engines have hidden issues. A reconditioned engine is strongly recommended - it includes new coolant lines, refurbished turbos, new coils and injectors, with a 12-24 month warranty. Used is cheaper (£4k-£7k) but factor in £2k-£4k for preventative work. Reconditioned addresses all known weak points and gives peace of mind.

Reconditioned: addresses all known weak points and gives peace of mind.

items.question: How do I confirm which N74B60 variant my car has?
items.answer: Check the engine code stamped on the block (left-hand side near the timing cover). The N74B60A (F-series, 2010-2015) uses the earlier DME and turbo actuator design. The N74B60B (G-series, 2016-2022) has updated software and improved cooling. The V5C logbook lists the full engine number. Variants are not interchangeable without full electronics transplant. ECU, wiring and cooling system differ between generations.
bullets: Variants are not interchangeable without full electronics transplant.
ECU, wiring and cooling system differ between generations.

items.question: How long does an N74B60 engine typically last?
items.answer: With meticulous maintenance and early preventative work, these engines can exceed 100,000-150,000 miles. The V12 is fundamentally well-engineered; the limiting factors are the plastic cooling components, ignition coils and fuel system components. Coolant line replacement recommended at 60k-80k miles as preventative. Ignition coil replacement at 60k-80k miles. Regular oil changes (5,000-8,000 miles) with BMW-spec oil are essential.

Regular oil changes (5,000‑8,000 miles) with BMW‑spec oil are essential.
